How are macros recursively expanded in C?

Direct Answer: Strictly speaking, they aren't. C macros are not recursive.

To prevent infinite loops during compilation, the C preprocessor "paints blue" (disables) any macro name that is currently expanding. If it encounters a macro name that is already in the expansion stack, it leaves it as plain text rather than expanding it again.

The "Painted Blue" Rule

This is the standard metaphor for C macro recursion. When a macro is currently being expanded, its name is added to a Hide Set (painted blue).

  • check_circle If the preprocessor encounters a "blue" token during a rescan, it treats it as raw text, not a macro.
  • check_circle This applies to the macro itself (direct recursion) and any macros currently in the call stack (indirect recursion).
  • check_circle Once expansion of that specific macro finishes, the paint is removed (unless it's still active in an outer layer).
layers

Argument Prescan

A common source of confusion is when arguments are expanded. The rule is simple but strict:

The General Flow:

  1. Prescan: Fully expand arguments unless they are operands of # or ##.
  2. Substitution: Replace parameters in the body with the (possibly expanded) arguments.
  3. Rescan: Scan the result again for more macros.

This is why you often see the #define STR(x) #x vs #define XSTR(x) STR(x) pattern to force expansion before stringification.
